newsitem.title: JAPAN: WW II sex slaves retell experience in Japan court.
newsitem.headline: WW II sex slaves retell experience in Japan court.

text.p: Filipino and and South Korean "comfort women" on Friday recounted how they were raped, brutalised and used as sex slaves by Japan's World War Two army.

In the first hearing of a class-action civil compensation case brought by 18 Filipina women, victims relived their time under Japanese rule in an effort to win 20 million yen each in compensation and a apology from the government.
In a separate hearing, a South Korean woman also told a court how she had been tricked into working for seven years in frontline military brothels during Japan's invasion of China.
Filipina plaintiff Cristeta Alcober opened her trial with an account of her capture at the age of 16 by Japanese soldiers.

"They burst into my house and took me and my 14-year-old cousin to the garrison. I was made to live with 30 other girls in a mud-floored, straw-roofed house which had barbed wire instead of walls," she told Tokyo District Court through an interpreter.
"On the third night, many of them raped me and when I resisted they stabbed my legs and back with their bayonets. I was covered in blood but they kept on raping me," she said, bursting into tears.
"After that, the soldiers raped me day and night. Sometimes nine of them in the evening and four or six in the afternoon... every day until I was released. That was when I was eighteen," she said.
Alcober and other victims were also forced to carry heavy rocks and sand during the daytime, she told the court.
The Filipinas' hearing on Friday was the 16th session of a case that began in 1993.
She is one of 200,000 Asian women historians estimate worked as "comfort women", the Japanese euphemism for women recruited to work in brothels for Japan's Imperial Army.
Japan only officially acknowledged the existence of the women in July 1992, and references to their plight appeared for the first time in Japanese school textbooks in April 1994.
Tokyo has not paid direct compensation to the women, saying all claims were settled by peace treaties that formally ended the war, and instead set up a private fund to offer reparations.
But a frail, 70-year-old Rosaria Nopueta raised the point most fiercely fought over between the Japanese government and supporters of the victims when she demanded an official apology.
"I want an apology and individual legal compensation from the Japanese government as soon as possible. We have been waiting a long time and it has still not come," she said.
Nopueta told how she saw Japanese troops slit the throats of her father, aunt and sister before she was taken to a garrison and violated by Japanese soldiers continuously for three months.

"When word went round the Americans had landed, the soldiers in the garrison took me and the other seven girls there out into the courtyard and slashed our necks. I was cut three times with a bayonet and left for dead," she added.
The fishmonger said she lived only because an acquaintance noticed her among the other corpses and rescued her.
In a separate civil case at Tokyo District Court, South Korean former comfort woman Son Shin-do said a 120 million yen damages claim was symbolic.
"I don't need the money. I just want an apology. Money can't buy back peoples' lives," she told the court.

"We were constantly on the move following the fighting and I could never rest. The soldiers beat me many times -- I still have scars on my back. I had many abortions and had to give away the only child I ever gave birth to," she said.
